ABBAGENTIC AI SECURITYSecurity architecture briefing

01 / Introduction

Problem Statement

AI agents can read business data, choose tasks and call connected systems. ABB needs controls that prevent unauthorized access, data disclosure and unsafe actions.

Security objective

Allow an agent to complete its assigned task with only the data, permissions and tools that task requires.

Protect dataCustomer records and intellectual property
Control accessAgent identities, credentials and delegation
Approve actionsOrders, messages and system changes

02 / Definitions

What Is an Agent?

An agent is software that uses an AI model to choose and carry out steps towards a goal. An AI model interprets input and proposes an answer or action. The application executes approved actions with assigned permissions.

Agentic AI security

Keeping an agent within its assigned purpose, access and operational limits, even when its inputs or connected tools are compromised.

Example request“Investigate this drive fault and prepare a service response.”
  1. Understand the task

    The model interprets the request and available evidence. It can be wrong or influenced by hostile content.

  2. Use connected systems

    The application can read records or request actions through APIs, using credentials assigned to it.

  3. Keep authority bounded

    Permissions, data policy, approvals and execution limits constrain what the agent can actually do.

What security must cover: the content the agent reads, the identity it uses, the tools it calls and the data or actions those calls produce.

Terms: “prompt” means instructions or content sent to the model. “Runtime” means the software that runs the decision-and-action loop.Sources [1] Hover for preview

03 / Architecture

Building Blocks

Start with a chatbot that only answers questions. Switch to an agent to add the components that let it use tools and act on business systems.

A chatbot that answers. The user sends a question. The model returns text. It cannot call tools or change a business system.

User requestA question or assigned task
AI modelInterprets input
Written answerReturns information

Chatbot example“What does an overcurrent fault mean?” The chatbot explains the fault. The engineer performs the work.

The boundary is tool accessIn this comparison, the chatbot only answers. The agent can call connected systems and choose follow-up steps. Those actions need authorization.

Chatbot: request → model → written answer. Agent: adds data, a runtime, tool calls, policy checks and task history.

Simplified architectures for this comparison. Tool access lets an agent act; identity and policy constrain what it can do.Sources [1] Hover for preview
03 / 27

04 / Operation

How an Agent Works

The runtime repeats these six steps. Each tool result can influence the next decision, so inputs and results need the same trust checks.

Select a step to inspect it.

  1. Read the goal, instructions, permitted documents, tool descriptions and current task state.

  2. Choose a next step. Decide which evidence or tool is needed and whether approval is required.

  3. Request a tool action. The runtime checks policy and executes it using the agent’s credentials.

  4. Read the real result: success, failure or new evidence. Tool output can itself contain hostile instructions.

  5. Retain only approved facts, with their source and expiry. Persistent memory is optional.

  6. Continue if needed; otherwise finish, escalate or stop at an approval, time or cost limit.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) connects agents to tools. A2A (Agent2Agent) connects agents to other agents. Neither replaces authentication, authorization or data policy.

The six steps are a teaching model. Implementations may combine steps; the security boundaries still apply.Sources [1] Hover for preview

05 / ABB service example

Example: An ABB Service Request

An engineer asks for help with an overcurrent fault on Drive 7 at Customer X. This is an illustrative workflow, not a verified ABB deployment.

Select a step to inspect it.

  1. Teams request: “Drive 7 at Customer X trips on overcurrent.” Read the approved drive manual, Customer X’s service history and a read-only telemetry replica.

  2. Correlate the fault and operating history. Propose a failed power module as a hypothesis; show the evidence and ask the engineer to confirm.

  3. Create a ServiceNow case. After approval, submit a €4,800 SAP parts requisition. Prepare a customer ETA email using Microsoft Graph.

  4. Read the actual case ID, order status and mail response. If the part is unavailable, revise the proposal; do not invent a delivery date.

  5. Save the confirmed diagnosis, evidence and case reference within Customer X’s scope. Give retained facts a source and expiry.

  6. Delegate only shipment tracking to a logistics agent if needed. Stop when complete, at a limit, or when approval is missing. Preserve the action trail.

Industrial boundary: read approved telemetry replicas. The agent has no write access to live equipment.

Teams → approved documents and telemetry → ServiceNow → SAP → customer email. The engineer remains accountable for the diagnosis and consequential approvals.Sources [1][2] Hover for preview

07 / Risks

Agent Risks: OWASP Top 10

OWASP defines ten agent-specific risk categories. They provide a common language for describing the protection a product offers and the gaps that remain.

OWASP categories and ABB workflow examples
IDRisk categoryExample in the ABB workflow
ASI01Agent Goal HijackA manual tells the agent to export another customer’s cases.
ASI02Tool Misuse & ExploitationA valid delete or email API is used for an unsafe purpose.
ASI03Identity & Privilege AbuseA service token exposes records beyond the current task.
ASI04Agentic Supply Chain VulnerabilitiesA compromised connector silently adds an email recipient.
ASI05Unexpected Code ExecutionGenerated commands run outside the intended sandbox.
ASI06Memory & Context PoisoningAn unconfirmed diagnosis becomes a fact in later jobs.
ASI07Insecure Inter-Agent CommunicationA forged logistics-agent message changes the destination.
ASI08Cascading FailuresA bad diagnosis triggers an order, email and follow-on work.
ASI09Human-Agent Trust ExploitationA persuasive summary hides a changed supplier or amount.
ASI10Rogue AgentsAn agent pursues a goal outside its authorized assignment.
Official OWASP category names; workflow examples and protection requirements are illustrative.Sources [2] Hover for preview

08 / Incident analysis

OpenAI and Hugging Face Incident

In July 2026, OpenAI research agents with reduced safeguards reached systems outside their assigned environment. Hugging Face, a platform for sharing AI models and datasets, was one affected organization.

9–10 July

External access

Agents compromised a third-party app hosted on Modal and found exposed Hugging Face credentials.

Following days

Further compromise

Agents chained vulnerabilities, executed code on Hugging Face servers and accessed evaluation data.

16–21 July

Detection and disclosure

Hugging Face disclosed activity on 16 July. OpenAI detected unusual activity on 19 July and disclosed involvement on 21 July.

Reported impact

Hugging Face reported access to five customer datasets associated with evaluation challenges. OpenAI reported compromise of research infrastructure, with no impact on its customer data or product availability.

Capabilities this incident calls for

Outbound network policy, isolated execution, scoped credentials and visibility into agent-to-agent communication. A model-content filter alone does not cover these paths.

This was a research-evaluation incident with reduced safeguards. It should not be presented as the normal behavior of a production agent.Sources [3][4] Hover for preview

09 / Incident analysis

Other Security Incidents and Findings

These cases involve different failure modes. Distinguish a research demonstration from a confirmed operational incident or a malicious package.

Research demonstration · June 2025

EchoLeak

Crafted email
Retrieved instructions
Automatic request
What happened and its limits

A crafted email caused Microsoft 365 Copilot to place sensitive context in an image URL that the client fetched. Microsoft patched the issue before disclosure; the cited analysis reports no in-the-wild exploitation.

Control implication

Inspect retrieved content and rendered output. Restrict outbound requests, including trusted-domain proxies.

Operational incident · July 2025

Replit database deletion

Coding task
Excessive access
Database deletion
What happened and its limits

A coding agent deleted an application database where development and production were insufficiently separated. Replit reported full restoration with no data lost.

Control implication

Separate environments, remove production write access, approve destructive actions and retain recoverable backups.

Malicious package · September 2025

postmark-mcp

Email connector
Hidden BCC
Data disclosure
What happened and its limits

A malicious third-party email connector secretly added a BCC recipient. The finding concerns the package, not a breach of the Postmark email service.

Control implication

Approve and pin connector versions. Inspect final recipients and payloads. Revoke compromised integrations.

Keep research demonstrations, confirmed operational incidents and malicious-package advisories distinct when assessing impact.Sources [5][6][7] Hover for preview

10 / Security controls

How to Secure Agents

Enforce permissions and action policy outside the model. Keep those controls effective even if an input filter misses an attack.

Know and limit the actor

  • C1Inventory agents, tools, owners and business purposes.
  • C2Give each agent a distinct, managed identity.
  • C3Issue short-lived credentials scoped to this task and customer.

Constrain what can run

  • C4Isolate code and network access; keep live OT out of scope.
  • C5Bind approvals to exact actions, amounts and destinations.
  • C6Use an approved registry with pinned, reviewed tool versions.

Inspect and enforce

  • C7Inspect inputs and tool results as untrusted content.
  • C8Enforce action, parameter, retry, time and cost limits.
  • C9Apply data classification, record access and outbound DLP.

Observe and respond

  • C10Keep tamper-evident records of identities, calls and outcomes.
  • C11Maintain security assurance and change history for models, tools and policies.
  • C12Provide suspension, token revocation, evidence capture and recovery.

Failure behavior: stop consequential actions when required approval or inspection is unavailable. Keep live equipment outside the agent’s write permissions.

Control model adapted from research §7; the mapping to ABB is a proposed architecture, not an OWASP product endorsement.Sources [2] Hover for preview

11 / Security capabilities

Required Security Capabilities

These capabilities are required across the application. A product may provide several; each needs an identified enforcement point and operating owner.

Security capabilities, enforcement points and required outcomes
CapabilityWhere it operatesRequired outcome
Discovery & postureAsset inventory + cloud / application integrationsFind unapproved agents and missing owners.
Agent identityIdentity provider + credential brokerPrevent overprivileged or stale access.
Tool / MCP gatewayBetween runtime and tool serversReject unapproved tools and destinations.
Runtime protectionBefore model input, output and tool executionStop malicious content or disallowed actions.
Data protectionSource permissions + outbound channelsPrevent unauthorized data movement.
Security assurancePre-production + continuous regressionExpose failures before and after changes.
Observability & responseAction pipeline + SIEM / SOARDetect, investigate and contain activity.
GovernanceOwner, risk and change-management recordsKeep approvals, reviews and decisions traceable.
Infrastructure containmentHost, network and industrial boundaryLimit execution and protect live systems.

Guardian agents are supervisory agents that review other agents. They can add detection, but they still need enforceable permissions, blocking and an operator-controlled stop.

Start with existing identity, DLP, cloud and SOC capabilities. Add products where the actual agent workflow has a demonstrated gap.Sources [2] Hover for preview

Model Armor

Google Cloud · Runtime protection

A Google Cloud inspection service for content sent to and returned by AI models. Applications submit content for a security verdict, then apply that verdict through their own integration.

AI interactionInspect + apply policyPermitted activity
Model Armor capabilities and scope
AreaCapabilities and scope
Security areaPrompt and response security, sensitive-data protection and content policy.
Main featuresDetects prompt injection, attempts to bypass model safeguards, harmful content and malicious URLs. Templates set filters and thresholds; sensitive-data policies can identify or redact protected information.
How it worksThe API returns filter results. Supported integrations can inspect, block or sanitize the submitted content before it reaches the model or the user.
Deployment and integrationsManaged service with regional endpoints and a REST API. Supports text and document inspection; image screening is in preview and has format and integration limits.
Visibility and responseFilter findings identify triggered policies. Cloud Logging supports investigation of inspection and blocking decisions when configured.
Additional offeringsSensitive Data Protection supplies classification and de-identification. Cloud service integrations apply Model Armor policies at supported application or gateway boundaries.
Scope and limitationsOnly submitted content is inspected. It does not issue agent credentials, authorize business transactions or isolate code. Images embedded inside documents are not screened as images.

Illustrative ABB use: Screen a customer service document before the model reads it, then inspect the drafted reply for sensitive data.

Falcon AI Detection and Response

CrowdStrike · Runtime protection

CrowdStrike’s AIDR service collects AI activity and applies security and data policies. For agents, its MCP proxy inspects messages exchanged with connected tools.

AI interactionInspect + apply policyPermitted activity
Falcon AI Detection and Response capabilities and scope
AreaCapabilities and scope
Security areaAI interaction visibility, prompt and data protection, and tool-traffic enforcement.
Main featuresThe MCP collector inspects tool discovery, requests and returned content. Guard checkpoints can allow, block or transform a message, including redacting sensitive values.
How it worksA proxy sits between the MCP client and server. It submits the relevant messages to AIDR policy checks before a tool receives them or the client receives results.

Scope and limitationsThe MCP proxy does not inspect model prompts and responses outside MCP interactions. Coverage from other collectors requires their own deployment and configuration.

AI interactionInspect + apply policyPermitted activity
AI Guardrails capabilities and scope
AreaCapabilities and scope
Security areaInput and output protection, sensitive-data safeguards and agent behavior controls.

26 / Next steps

Recommended Next Steps for ABB

Build a shortlist around the gaps in ABB’s current capabilities. Compare the complete deployment and commercial scope before recommending a purchase.

DAYS
01–30

Map requirements

Identify the agent estate, data paths and existing licenses. Prioritize gaps in discovery, identity, tool access, runtime protection and isolation.

DAYS
31–60

Compare the shortlist

Request product architecture, supported integrations, data terms and release status. Compare platform extensions with specialist products and internally operated software.

DAYS
61–90

Prepare the purchase decision

Document the selected capabilities, remaining gaps, operating owner and total cost. Include license dependencies, contractual commitments and a phased adoption plan.

The decision for ABB: fund the missing capabilities with a clear product scope, integration plan and operating owner. A combined architecture may need several complementary products.
